items.canonical_answer: It reveals costs borne outside the firm’s transaction (1), because private profit alone may omit effects on households and the wider net outcome (1).

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of judging a project solely by its immediate private profit.
items.canonical_answer: Future or third-party effects may be omitted (1), because the firm’s current net receipts do not measure all relevant interests or periods (1).

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a resource project should proceed when it offers current jobs but may impose lasting harm on nearby residents and future access is uncertain.
items.canonical_answer: Argument for: useful output and work can support current income and opportunities. Argument against: third-party harm and depletion can reduce wider welfare and future options, which private returns may omit. Judgement: compare feasible harm-reducing alternatives, relevant social effects and credible resource conditions. Proceed only if the evidenced net gains and safeguards justify the costs; jobs alone do not establish that condition.
marking_guidance: Argument for: current productive gains up to 3; argument against: external/future costs up to 3; judgement with evidence and resource condition up to 2=8.

items.prompt: A processing project has private resource cost N$80,000 and estimated external cost N$20,000 for the same period. It offers current work, but some residents face noise. A modification would reduce harm while adding private cost; its full figures are not supplied. (a) Describe three relevant cost or interest features (6). (b) Examine what can be concluded about the project and modification (7). (c) Suggest a justified decision process (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Private cost is borne directly, external cost affects third parties, and social cost is N$100,000 under the stated estimates. (b) Work can support current income while noise burdens residents. The modification may improve the wider outcome if harm reduction exceeds added relevant cost, but no precise net comparison is possible without values and scope. Private cost alone and external cost alone each omit part of the total. (c) Obtain comparable modification costs and harm evidence, consider timing and groups, and compare feasible alternatives. The judgement should prioritise an evidenced wider net outcome and workable harm controls rather than infer approval from jobs or rejection from any harm alone.
marking_guidance: Context: project. Parts/allocation: (a) private, external, total 2 each=6. (b) group mechanism 3, modification condition 2, scope/data limit 2=7. (c) comparable evidence 3, feasible options 2, supported judgement 2=7. Mechanism: different groups and periods carry gains and burdens; judgement compares evidenced net effects.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: (a) Define social cost (2). (b) Explain private versus external benefit (2). (c) Explain why timing matters (2). (d) Explain use versus overuse (2). (e) Define a tariff (2). (f) Define a quota (2). (g) Explain public versus private spending (2). (h) Explain why ownership alone does not establish effectiveness (2).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Private plus external costs on a consistent basis. (b) Private accrues directly to the decision-maker; external benefits third parties. (c) Immediate gains can coexist with future burdens or current sacrifices with later gains. (d) Rate/method and resource conditions determine damage, not the fact of use alone. (e) Tax on imports. (f) Restriction on import quantity. (g) Government decision-maker versus households/private organisations. (h) Need, incentives, costs and actual delivery matter under either arrangement.
marking_guidance: Parts/allocation and precision: eight at 2. (a) private + external; (b) recipient boundary; (c) period contrast and consequence; (d) use plus conditions; (e) tax + imports; (f) quantity + import restriction; (g) decision-maker distinction; (h) ownership versus outcome conditions.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: An authority considers a temporary import tariff to support local producers. Domestic buyers and firms using the imported input oppose higher costs. Supporters claim future jobs will justify any present expense, but no viability timetable or cost estimates are supplied. (a) Define a tariff (2). (b) Explain two groups’ conflicting interests (4). (c) Explain the possible short- and long-term effects (7). (d) Discuss whether the supporters’ claim is sufficient (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Tax on imports. (b) Protected producers may gain demand or time to develop. Buyers and input-using firms may pay more or face less choice. (c) Current support can preserve selected activity while higher input costs affect other production. Longer-term benefits depend on improved viability, not merely the temporary label. Weak rivalry, ongoing dependence or responses abroad can add costs. The distribution of jobs and gains is not uniform. (d) Possible development is a relevant case for support, but the claim that future jobs justify any present cost is unsupported. Seek credible viability evidence, duration, costs and alternatives. Support is justified only if the expected wider gains and feasible conditions warrant the burdens; current information does not establish that.
marking_guidance: Context: tariff. Parts/allocation: (a) tax 1, imports 1. (b) two group effects 2 each=4. (c) present mechanism 3, future conditions 2, distribution/risks 2=7. (d) benefit case 2, evidence/absolute limit 2, conditional judgement 3=7. Mechanism: different groups and periods carry gains and burdens; judgement compares evidenced net effects.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a council should prefer a public service to a private option solely because its stated aim is social benefit, when costs, access and delivery evidence are incomplete (9).
items.canonical_answer: For: public provision can pursue access and wider outcomes that individual purchases may leave unresolved. Against: a stated aim does not prove effective delivery, and public resources have alternative uses. Private provision can meet some needs, while either option may have distributional and external effects. Judgement: compare feasible arrangements on useful service, access, complete costs and accountability over a suitable period. The condition is evidence that the chosen arrangement meets the need more effectively relative to resources and alternatives; public ownership or private status alone does not settle it.
marking_guidance: Argument for: wider-access mechanism up to 4. Argument against: opportunity cost/delivery and alternative limits up to 4. Judgement: distinct effective-service and resource condition 1. Total 9. Condition: actual access and delivery relative to complete costs must support the choice.

items.prompt: Explain why a government subsidy to domestic producers can help them compete with imports.
items.canonical_answer: The subsidy can reduce domestic producers’ effective cost per unit (1), enabling them to offer a lower price and compete more strongly with imports if they pass the saving to buyers (1).
marking_guidance: Reason: reduction in domestic producers’ effective unit cost (1); because/link: this can support a lower competitive price if savings are passed on (1). A subsidy does not guarantee efficient production or increased sales.
